templates.pattern: A patient produces [VOL] mL of urine in [TIME] minutes. Calculate the glomerular filtration rate in mL/min.
templates.explanation:
Glomerular filtration rate = volume filtered ÷ time
= [VOL] ÷ [TIME]
= [RESULT] mL/min

Normal GFR is 90-120 mL/min. A GFR below 60 mL/min for more than 3 months indicates chronic kidney disease. GFR declines naturally with age.

templates.pattern: A patient has a pulse pressure of [PP] mmHg and an arterial compliance of [C] mL/mmHg. Calculate the stroke volume in mL.
templates.explanation:
Stroke volume = pulse pressure × arterial compliance
= [PP] × [C]
= [RESULT] mL

Arterial compliance describes how much the aorta expands per mmHg of pressure. Normal stroke volume is 60-100 mL. Stiff arteries (low compliance) in older patients produce a wider pulse pressure for the same stroke volume.

templates.pattern: A patient has a systolic blood pressure of [SYS] mmHg and a diastolic blood pressure of [DIA] mmHg. Calculate the mean arterial pressure in mmHg.
templates.explanation:
Mean arterial pressure = diastolic + (pulse pressure ÷ 3)
= [DIA] + ([SYS] − [DIA]) ÷ 3
= [DIA] + [PP] ÷ 3
= [RESULT] mmHg

MAP represents the average pressure driving blood through the circulation. Normal MAP is 70-100 mmHg. Below 60 mmHg organ perfusion becomes inadequate.

templates.pattern: A person breathes with a tidal volume of [TV] mL and a respiratory rate of [RR] breaths per minute. Calculate the pulmonary ventilation rate in mL/min.
templates.explanation:
Pulmonary ventilation = tidal volume × respiratory rate
= [TV] × [RR]
= [RESULT] mL/min

Normal pulmonary ventilation at rest is about 6000 mL/min. This is the total air moved in and out of the lungs per minute. It differs from alveolar ventilation because it includes dead space air that does not reach the alveoli.

templates.pattern: A person has a basal metabolic rate of [BMR] kcal/day and a physical activity level of [AF]. Calculate their total daily energy requirement in kcal/day.
templates.explanation:
Total energy requirement = BMR × activity factor
= [BMR] × [AF]
= [RESULT] kcal/day

Activity factors: sedentary=1.2, lightly active=1.4, moderately active=1.6, very active=1.8, extremely active=2.0-2.2. Athletes may need over 5000 kcal/day.

templates.pattern: A drug has an initial concentration of [C0] mg/L. After [TIME] hours the concentration is [C1] mg/L. The concentration has halved [N] times. Calculate the half life of the drug in hours.
templates.explanation:
Half life = total time ÷ number of halvings
= [TIME] ÷ [N]
= [RESULT] hours

Half life is constant for a given drug regardless of initial concentration. Drugs with long half lives accumulate in the body with repeated doses. Short half life drugs are cleared quickly.

templates.pattern: A patient's lung volume increases by [DV] mL in response to a transpulmonary pressure change of [DP] cmH₂O. Calculate the lung compliance in mL/cmH₂O.
templates.explanation:
Lung compliance = change in volume ÷ change in pressure
= [DV] ÷ [DP]
= [RESULT] mL/cmH₂O

Normal lung compliance is about 200 mL/cmH₂O. Compliance is reduced in pulmonary fibrosis making the lungs stiff and hard to inflate. It is increased in emphysema where alveolar walls are destroyed.

templates.pattern: Blood contains [HB] g/dL of haemoglobin with an oxygen saturation of [SAT]%. Each gram of haemoglobin carries 1.34 mL of O₂ at full saturation. Calculate the oxygen content of blood in mL O₂/dL.
templates.explanation:
O₂ content = Hb × saturation × 1.34 ÷ 100
= [HB] × [SAT] × 1.34 ÷ 100
= [RESULT] mL O₂/dL

Normal arterial O₂ content is about 20 mL/dL. Anaemia (low Hb) and low saturation both reduce oxygen delivery to tissues.

templates.pattern: A spirometry test shows an inspiratory reserve volume of [IRV] mL, a tidal volume of [TV] mL and an expiratory reserve volume of [ERV] mL. Calculate the vital capacity in mL.
templates.explanation:
Vital capacity = IRV + tidal volume + ERV
= [IRV] + [TV] + [ERV]
= [RESULT] mL

Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after maximum inhalation. Normal values are 3500-5000 mL. It is reduced in restrictive lung diseases.

templates.pattern: A person has a BMI of [BMI] and an age of [AGE] years. Using the simplified formula, estimate their body fat percentage. (Body fat % = 1.2 × BMI + 0.23 × age − 5.4 for males)
templates.explanation:
Body fat % = 1.2 × BMI + 0.23 × age − 5.4
= 1.2 × [BMI] + 0.23 × [AGE] − 5.4
= [1.2*BMI] + [0.23*AGE] − 5.4
= [RESULT]%

Body fat percentage is a better measure of health risk than BMI alone. Healthy ranges for males are 10-20% and for females 18-28%.
